title: Chanticleer and the Fox
text:
In a poor widow's farmyard lived a splendid rooster named Chanticleer, the finest crower in the land, with his favorite hen, Pertelote. One night he dreamed of a reddish beast that tried to seize him. Pertelote scolded him for being afraid of dreams and told him to take a laxative. He argued long and learnedly that dreams can be warnings, but in the end he forgot his fear and strutted about the yard.

A fox named Russell had slipped into the garden and lay hidden among the herbs. When Chanticleer spotted him and was about to flee, the fox spoke kindly. He had only come, he said, to hear Chanticleer sing. He had known his father, whose singing was magnificent: he used to close his eyes, stand on tiptoe and stretch out his neck to crow. Could the son do as well?

Chanticleer, flattered, shut his eyes and stretched his neck, and the fox seized him by the throat and ran for the woods. The widow, her daughters, the dogs and the whole farm chased after them, shouting.

In the fox's jaws, Chanticleer had an idea. He suggested that the fox turn and taunt his pursuers. The fox liked the idea and opened his mouth to speak. Chanticleer broke free and flew up into a tree. The fox tried flattery again, but the rooster had learned his lesson and stayed where he was.
lesson: Flattery works best when you are tired of being careful. If someone praises you into closing your eyes, open them. And an opponent's own vanity can be your way out.
source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Nun's Priest's Tale
